newsitem.title: CHINA: Suicide bomb kills one, second blast in S. China.
newsitem.headline: Suicide bomb kills one, second blast in S. China.

text.p: A man blew himself up with a home-made bomb in a Beijing park just metres from the heart of China's government and police on Wednesday said the latest explosion to rock China's capital was a suicide.

The man who died was from central Hunan province and had set off the blast that killed him in a quiet corner of Zhongshan park in central Beijing at 4.50 p.m. (0850 GMT) on Tuesday, Liu Wei, assistant spokesman to the Beijing city public security bureau told reporters.
The man had left a suicide note, Liu said, but declined to give details of the contents of the letter.

No other casualties were reported in the explosion in the park that lies in the western corner of the Forbidden City, former palace of China's emperors, and just across the road from the Great Hall of the People where China's leaders meet.
"It looks as if it was definitely a suicide and the damage was limited," a park official said.
It was the third bomb explosion reported in China's capital in just two months.

Police have already been on high alert in Beijing since a bomb exploded on a bus during rush hour in a central shopping district on March 7, injuring several people. The blast came just days after another, smaller explosion.
In southern Guangdong province, police said five people were killed and six wounded in an explosion on a bus on Monday.
That blast occurred in the rear of a local bus in the town of Shunde, officials said.
The explosion was set off by a young man and a young woman, both of whom were killed in the blast, local officials said.
"We are investigating the cause of the explosion," one police official said, adding that it was not clear whether the blast was a suicide.

China's state media has regularly reported explosions aboard buses and trains, most caused by accidents involving travellers illegally carrying industrial-use explosives, which are easily available in China.

Police in China's capital are nervous of bomb attacks that could damage security in the city in the run-up to the anniversary of the June 4, 1989, bloody military crackdown on student-led pro-democracy demonstrations as well as the July 1 resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong.

The bomb attacks in Beijing have stunned China's leadership, which has been trying to put on a show of stability and solidarity after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on February 19, and in the run-up to the handover of Hong Kong.
City officials have said the bombings in Beijing were not linked to earlier attacks in the restive, mainly Moslem region of Xinjiang.

Nine people were killed and 74 injured when three bus bombings rocked Xinjiang's regional capital, Urumqi, on February 25 in an attack that coincided with final funeral rites in Beijing on that day for Deng.
